subject: Polity
description: Parliamentary privileges in India — collective and individual privileges of MPs, Articles 105 and 194, breach of privilege, contempt of House.

questions.stem: Which Article of the Indian Constitution deals with PARLIAMENTARY PRIVILEGES of MPs?
questions.explanation: ARTICLE 105 of the Constitution — PRIVILEGES OF the HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT and THEIR MEMBERS. KEY PROVISIONS: (1) FREEDOM OF SPEECH in Parliament: MPs CANNOT be sued in any court for anything they say in Parliament or its committees (Art 105(2)). (2) IMMUNITY for VOTES — MPs aren't liable for any vote cast in Parliament or committees. (3) RIGHT TO PUBLISH proceedings — under authority of either House, no one can be sued. (4) Other privileges 'as may from time to time be defined by Parliament by law' — Parliament hasn't enacted a comprehensive law, so privileges remain those of UK House of Commons (1950) + judicial decisions. ARTICLE 194 — CORRESPONDING privileges for STATE LEGISLATURES. TYPES: (1) COLLECTIVE PRIVILEGES — of the House: right to publish proceedings, exclude strangers, regulate own procedures, punish for contempt. (2) INDIVIDUAL PRIVILEGES — of MPs: freedom of speech, freedom from arrest in CIVIL cases (NOT criminal) during 40 days before/after session + during session. CONFLICT: parliamentary privileges + judicial review have led to DEBATES (e.g., Karnataka MLAs disqualification 2019). PYQ FREQUENCY: Art 105 in UPSC, MPSC, state PSC.

questions.stem: Members of Parliament have FREEDOM FROM ARREST in:

options.option_text: All criminal cases at all times

questions.explanation: MPs have FREEDOM FROM ARREST ONLY IN CIVIL CASES — and only DURING the 40 DAYS BEFORE the session, the SESSION itself, and 40 DAYS AFTER it ends. CRIMINAL CASES — NO IMMUNITY: MPs CAN be arrested for criminal offences at ANY time (e.g., murder, corruption, bribery). ALSO NO IMMUNITY for: (1) Preventive detention. (2) Civil proceedings other than arrest (e.g., service of summons). (3) Cases under the Indian Penal Code. NOTABLE CASE — JMM BRIBERY CASE (1998): SC held that MPs accepting bribes for VOTES IN PARLIAMENT were NOT immune from prosecution under Art 105. RECENT 2024 — MP Sita Soren CASE: SC OVERTURNED the JMM case via a 7-judge bench (Sita Soren v. Union of India, March 2024) — held that NO IMMUNITY for MPs/MLAs against bribery prosecution, even if related to votes/speeches in House. This was a major judicial pivot. ENTERING & SEARCHING PARLIAMENT: police cannot enter parliament premises without speaker's consent. ATTACHED PRIVILEGE: MPs cannot be summoned by court when Parliament is in session (must seek leave of House). PYQ FREQUENCY: arrest immunity is a top UPSC, MPSC MCQ — 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: BREACH OF PARLIAMENTARY PRIVILEGE refers to:
questions.explanation: BREACH OF PRIVILEGE — any ACT that DISREGARDS or VIOLATES privileges of the House or its Members. Parliament can punish such breaches as 'CONTEMPT OF THE HOUSE'. EXAMPLES: (1) Publishing FALSE/MISLEADING reports of proceedings. (2) Insulting/intimidating MPs in connection with their parliamentary duties. (3) Disturbing parliamentary proceedings (e.g., shouting from gallery). (4) Refusing to appear before a committee when summoned. (5) Misleading a parliamentary committee with false testimony. (6) Bribery of MPs (now NO immunity per Sita Soren 2024). PROCEDURE for breach allegations: (1) MP raises issue in House; presiding officer (Speaker/Chairman) decides if it should go to PRIVILEGES COMMITTEE. (2) Committee investigates, calls evidence. (3) Recommends action. (4) House takes final decision — admonishment, reprimand, suspension, EVEN IMPRISONMENT (rare). NOTABLE CASE: 2005 'CASH FOR QUESTIONS' SCANDAL — 11 MPs caught taking bribes for questions; expelled from Parliament. PARLIAMENTARY ETHICS COMMITTEE handles ethical lapses (different from privileges committee). PYQ FREQUENCY: breach-of-privilege concept in UPSC, state PSC polity 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: An MP's IMMUNITY for SPEECH in the House extends to:

options.option_text: Speeches given outside in public rallies
All public statements made by MPs

questions.explanation: FREEDOM OF SPEECH (Art 105(2)) — MPs CANNOT be sued in any court for ANYTHING they say in Parliament or its committees. This is BROAD: covers debates, questions, speeches, comments — even if they are FALSE, DEFAMATORY, or INFLAMMATORY. RATIONALE: ensures fearless representation; MPs need not censor themselves for fear of litigation. KEY LIMITS: (1) Outside Parliament — NO IMMUNITY: speeches at public rallies, social media posts, press interviews ARE subject to defamation laws. (2) Within Parliament, subject to Rules of Procedure: presiding officer can call MPs to order, expunge unparliamentary words, suspend the speaker. (3) Bribery for speeches: SC's 2024 Sita Soren judgment — bribery prosecutable (no immunity). HISTORICAL EXAMPLES: (1) Derogatory statements in Parliament that would be defamation outside — fully protected. (2) JNU 'tukde-tukde' debates — speech inside Parliament safe; speeches at JNU campus are not. UNPARLIAMENTARY LANGUAGE LIST (LS Secretariat) — Speaker maintains a registry of words to be expunged: 'I will not say' lists in past included 'turncoat', 'jumla', etc. PYQ ANGLE: speech immunity tested in UPSC, MPSC 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests boundaries of constitutional protection.

questions.stem: The Sita Soren case (2024) is a landmark judgment regarding:

options.option_text: Bribery for parliamentary votes/speeches not immune

questions.explanation: SITA SOREN v. UNION OF INDIA (March 2024) — a 7-judge SC Constitution Bench unanimously OVERTURNED the 1998 JMM Bribery Case ruling. NEW POSITION: PARLIAMENTARY PRIVILEGE under Art 105 does NOT extend to BRIBERY for VOTES OR SPEECHES — MPs/MLAs CAN be prosecuted criminally for accepting illegal gratification. KEY REASONING: (a) Privilege under Art 105(2) is for 'speech and votes' — not for ACCEPTING BRIBES related to them. (b) Bribery is COMPLETED at the moment of taking money, BEFORE the speech/vote happens — so the act of bribery itself is OUTSIDE the protected zone. (c) Any other reading would create a 'license to corruption' for legislators. CASE BACKGROUND: Sita Soren (Hemant Soren's sister-in-law, JMM legislator) was alleged to have accepted bribe to vote for a particular Rajya Sabha candidate from Jharkhand in 2012 — but voted differently. Initial ruling (per JMM 1998) gave her immunity. Now overturned. IMPLICATIONS: (1) Future legislator bribery cases will proceed in court. (2) ED/CBI cases on MPs become more enforceable. (3) Senior counsel debates have flagged need for clearer law of legislative privileges. PYQ FREQUENCY: 2024-26 papers will likely include this case in UPSC, MPSC, state PSC.

questions.stem: Which Article of the Constitution provides PRIVILEGES for STATE LEGISLATURES (similar to Art 105 for Parliament)?
questions.explanation: ARTICLE 194 — PRIVILEGES of STATE LEGISLATURES and their members. Mirror of Article 105 (which applies to Parliament). KEY PROVISIONS: (1) Freedom of speech in state legislature. (2) Right to publish proceedings. (3) Other privileges as defined by state legislature (or as enjoyed by UK House of Commons in 1950). PARALLEL STRUCTURE: Art 105 (Centre) ↔ Art 194 (States); Art 79 (Parliament constitution) ↔ Art 168 (state legislature constitution); Art 99 (oath/affirmation) ↔ Art 188 (state); Art 100 (voting + quorum) ↔ Art 189 (state). POWERS of STATE LEGISLATURES: (a) Pass state laws (List II, III subjects). (b) Approve state budget. (c) Hold executive accountable. (d) Initiate impeachment-related processes (HC judges). NOTABLE CASE: 1964 KESHAV SINGH CASE — clash between UP Vidhan Sabha and Allahabad HC over the Vidhan Sabha's privilege to send a person to jail. SC held that PRIVILEGES + Fundamental Rights must be HARMONIZED; courts can review whether a privilege violated FRs. PRIVILEGES vs. FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS: ongoing tension; constitution amendment proposed but never enacted to clarify. PYQ FREQUENCY: Art 194 mirror in UPSC, state PSC polity — 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: An MP CANNOT be served a court summons:

options.option_text: At any place at any time freely
Even at home for criminal cases
While not in actual session ever

questions.explanation: MPs are protected from being SERVED with court PROCESSES (summons, warrants, etc.) WITHIN the precincts of Parliament during sessions WITHOUT prior permission of the SPEAKER (LS) or CHAIRMAN (RS). This is a COLLECTIVE PRIVILEGE of the House — to PROTECT its dignity and prevent disruption of proceedings. KEY POINTS: (1) Outside Parliament premises: MP can be served normally (at home, office). (2) Inside Parliament: requires Speaker's prior nod. (3) Police can't enter Parliament without Speaker's consent for arrest, search, seizure. PRECEDENTS: (a) An arrest warrant for an MP — police must inform Speaker first; Speaker decides whether/how it'll be served. (b) Civil summons — same protocol. RECENT EVENTS: 2008 'cash-for-vote' scandal — speaker permitted CBI access to certain documents but limited interference. RELATED PRIVILEGES: (1) Right to EXCLUDE STRANGERS from House (e.g., gallery passes are revocable). (2) Right to REGULATE OWN PROCEDURES (per Articles 118 and 208 — Parliament/legislature makes its own Rules). (3) Right to PUNISH CONTEMPT (rarely used; in 2007 the LS suspended MP Suresh Kalmadi for misconduct). PYQ ANGLE: parliamentary precincts privilege in UPSC, MPSC 1× per 2 cycles.
